blocks.heading: Job, batch and flow production
blocks.text: Job production makes a single product at a time, usually to the customer’s exact specification. Batch production makes a group of similar units before changing to another group. Flow production moves standardised units through a continuous sequence of stages. Compare volume, variety and sequence: customised one-off work differs from repeated groups and from a continuously operating standard line. Job production can offer flexibility with high skill and time per unit; batches balance variety and repetition but require changeovers; flow can support high volume but needs dependable demand, coordination and equipment. A flow line does not guarantee lower unit cost if capacity is underused or coordination and breakdown costs offset savings.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Omi Furniture makes one customised cabinet; fictional Kena Bakery makes groups of different loaf types; fictional Hila Bottles operates a continuous standard bottling line. These respectively illustrate job, batch and flow. The product’s name alone does not determine the method; describe how the stated process handles units.

blocks.heading: Job production
blocks.text: Job production makes a single product at a time, usually to the customer’s exact specifications. It suits custom variety and skilled flexible work, with close attention to individual requirements. It can take longer and have a high cost per unit compared with suitable repeated work. Batch production instead groups similar units; flow runs standardised units through an ongoing sequence. A business can use different methods for different orders.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Teya Joinery makes a cabinet measured for one unusual room. Skilled individual work fits the exact dimensions, but time and price must cover that effort. A standard line would need adaptation to deliver the same variety.

blocks.heading: Batch production
blocks.text: Batch production makes a group of similar items before changing to another group. It can combine repeated work within a batch with variety between batches. Setup and cleaning between groups take time and work may wait between stages. Job production focuses on individual specifications; flow focuses on a continuous standard sequence. Suitable batch size depends on demand, equipment and the cost of holding stock.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Omi Bakery makes a batch of one loaf type, changes its setup and then makes a different loaf type. Repeated groups with a changeover identify batch production, not a continuously unchanged flow. It can supply variety but needs planned timing to avoid excessive waiting.

blocks.heading: Flow production
blocks.text: Flow production moves standardised units continuously through a sequence of operations. It can support high output and consistent processes, but usually needs substantial equipment, dependable demand and coordination between stages. A breakdown can disrupt the line, and limited variety may not suit customised orders. Lower unit cost depends on capacity use and on coordination and other diseconomies not offsetting potential savings. Job and batch production provide different flexibility and volume patterns.

blocks.heading: Putting the idea to work
blocks.text: Fictional Hila Bottles has continuing demand for identical filled bottles and a coordinated line. Flow may fit its standard volume. If demand falls and the line sits idle, fixed commitments and coordination costs can undermine the expected unit-cost benefit.

blocks.heading: Keeping the ideas apart
blocks.text:
Explain the methods at three fictional workshops: one makes a unique measured gate; another makes a group of one design then changes design; a third runs identical units through a continuing line.

The unique specification is job production; repeated groups with changeovers are batch; the ongoing standard sequence is flow. The material or business size alone does not identify the method.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Production method, scale and location
blocks.text:
Fictional Eha Gates makes custom gates for nearby households. Each order has different dimensions. Skilled workers and suitable premises are available locally. A foreign site offers lower rent but would delay measuring and installation, which customers require quickly. No large standard contract exists.

a(i) Define job production. [2]
a(ii) State two location factors relevant to a manufacturer. [2]
b State two characteristics of batch production. [2]
c Explain why job production fits Eha’s orders better than a standard flow line. [6]
d Evaluate the local site against the lower-rent foreign site. [8]

a(i) A single product is made at a time, usually to the customer’s exact specification. a(ii) Suitable skills and transport access. b Similar items are made in groups and changeovers occur between groups. c Different gate dimensions need flexible skilled work and individual attention. A standard line would restrict variety and has no dependable large standard demand to use its capacity. d Local skills and quick measurement/installation fit a stated essential service need. The foreign rent saving is attractive but does not replace access and may create delay and extra coordination. Remain local on these facts, while comparing full relevant costs and recognising that a different service need could favour another location.

blocks.heading: Worked practice: Production method, scale and location
blocks.text:
Fictional Nara Cabinets receives varied custom orders requiring local measurement. It has skilled workers and suitable local premises. It compares job production near customers with a distant standard flow line whose lower stated rent is offset by slow customer contact.

Evaluate Nara’s local job-production option against its distant flow alternative under the original facts. Give a concise plan. [12]

Requirements: varying dimensions and local measurement. Job/local option: flexible skills and quick contact; may involve high labour time per item. Flow/distant option: standard output and lower stated rent, but loses custom flexibility and responsiveness. Unit-cost advantages would need sufficient standard demand, used capacity and controlled coordination or other diseconomies. Judgement: retain local job production while the custom need is decisive.
